newsitem.title: GERMANY: Weakening mark, rate fears continue to hound Bunds.
newsitem.headline: Weakening mark, rate fears continue to hound Bunds.

text.p: German Bunds spiralled lower for the fourth session in a row on Tuesday as the mark continued to be battered lower against the dollar.

Analysts said that comments from the Munich-based ifo economic research institute saying that European central banks were coming under pressure to consider tightening interest rates to support their currencies increased tension in the German debt market.
"We're were okay at the open, but after the Ifo comments prices took quite a hit," said a London-based futures trader.
Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing added to the market's jitters, telling a German weekly magazine in an interview that the Bundesbank was concerned about the pace of the marks' decline.
Traders say Issing and Ifo combined had fueled a resurgence in speculation that the Bundesbank may move to tighten short-term rates in the coming weeks if the mark fails to stabilise.
The mark hit an eight-year low against the dollar earlier on Tuesday, but recovered somewhat after Issing's comments and was trading at 1.8773 marks to the dollar at 1439 GMT.

One analyst said Issing's words were a signal to the markets that the Bundesbank's patience had run out, adding that he thought the likelihood of either foreign exchange intervention or a repo rate move was now more than 50 percent.
The DTB September Bund future was 46 basis points lower on the day at 101.70 by 1446 GMT, while the December futures contract was down 36 basis points at 100.98.
In the cash market, the 10-year Bund had shed 46 basis points to stand at 102.09 for a bid yield of 5.708 percent.
Looking ahead, traders said Bunds will continue to be hounded by the possibility of a Bundesbank rate move, with all eyes fixed firmly on dollar/mark.

"If we carry on seeing moves like we did today (in the mark), there is practically no chance that Bunds can recover much until we have a better idea of whethre the Bundesbank will do anything about it," said the London trader.
An Ifo economist said earlier that "alarm bells" would start ringing at the Bundesbank if the dollar were to go beyond 1.90 marks.
